lessons.title: The structure of fruit trees and vines
lessons.html:
The structure of fruit trees and vines

A foreman who understands how a tree or vine is built and how it works can make better decisions about pruning, thinning, irrigation and spraying, and can explain to workers why each task matters.

Roots

Roots anchor the plant and take up water and nutrients. Most of the active feeding roots of orchard trees and vines are in the upper part of the soil, within the wetted zone of drippers or micro-sprinklers. Roots need oxygen: waterlogged soils, compaction by tractors and poor drainage kill roots and lead to root diseases such as Phytophthora.

Rootstock and scion

Most commercial fruit trees and vines are grafted. The rootstock provides the roots and is chosen for soil, vigour, drought tolerance and resistance to pests such as phylloxera in grapes or nematodes. The scion is the cultivar that gives the fruit, for example Packham's Triumph pear, Golden Delicious apple or Chenin blanc grape. The graft union must stay above the soil, or the scion may root and lose the rootstock's benefits.

Trunk, branches and shoots

The trunk and framework branches carry water up through the xylem and sugars down through the phloem, which lies just under the bark. Damage to the bark from implements, sunburn or ring-barking cuts the phloem and starves the roots.

Buds

  • Vegetative buds grow into shoots and leaves.
  • Flower or mixed buds produce flowers and fruit. In apples and pears many are on spurs; in stone fruit, many are on one-year-old shoots; in grapes, the fruitful buds are on the shoots arising from one-year-old canes.

Knowing where the fruit buds are is the basis of correct pruning for each crop.

Leaves

Leaves are the factory of the plant. They capture sunlight, take in carbon dioxide through stomata and lose water through transpiration.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis, respiration and water
lessons.html:
Photosynthesis, respiration and water

Photosynthesis

In the green leaf, chlorophyll uses light energy to combine carbon dioxide from the air and water from the roots into sugars, releasing oxygen. These sugars feed shoot growth, root growth, fruit and the reserves stored in wood and roots for next season. More well-lit, healthy leaf area means more sugar - which is why canopy management and leaf health are so important.

Respiration

All living cells burn sugar to release energy for growth and maintenance. Respiration continues day and night and increases with temperature. Very hot nights use up sugar that could have gone into fruit. After harvest, fruit keeps respiring, which is why fast cooling extends shelf life.

Transpiration and water uptake

Water evaporates from leaves through the stomata, pulling water up from the roots through the xylem. This also cools the leaf. When soil water runs low, the plant closes its stomata to save water; this also stops carbon dioxide entering, so photosynthesis slows. Ongoing water stress reduces fruit size, shoot growth and next year's bud development.

Translocation and sinks

Sugars move through the phloem from sources (mature leaves) to sinks (growing shoots, fruit, roots). Fruit is a strong sink. Too many fruit on a tree means each one gets less and stays small - this is why thinning improves fruit size. Too much vigorous shoot growth competes with fruit for sugar and shades the canopy.

Light in the canopy

Leaves deep in a dense canopy receive little light and may use more sugar than they produce. Shaded buds are also less fruitful, and shaded fruit colours poorly. Pruning, summer pruning, shoot positioning and training systems aim to bring light into the canopy evenly.

lessons.title: Growth stages, dormancy and plant hormones
lessons.html:
Growth stages, dormancy and plant hormones

The seasonal cycle

StageWhat happens
Dormancy (winter)Leaves dropped; buds resting; reserves in wood and roots
Bud break (spring)Buds swell and open, using stored reserves
FloweringPollination and fertilisation set fruit
Fruit set and cell divisionFruit cells multiply rapidly
Cell enlargementFruit grows in size; water and sugar move in
Ripening and harvestSugar rises, acid drops, colour develops, flesh softens
Post-harvestLeaves rebuild reserves before leaf fall

The post-harvest period is often neglected but important: healthy leaves after harvest fill the reserves that drive next spring's bud break and flowering.

Chilling requirement

Deciduous fruit trees need a period of winter cold to break dormancy evenly. In warm winters in parts of the Western Cape and other regions, insufficient chilling causes uneven, delayed bud break and poor flowering. Growers may then use rest-breaking agents according to label and advice from their consultant.

Pollination

Many apple, pear, plum and cherry cultivars need a compatible pollinator cultivar planted nearby, and bees to carry pollen. Most grape cultivars are self-pollinating. Pesticides must be applied in ways that protect bees during flowering, following the label.

Plant hormones

  • Auxins - made in shoot tips; control apical dominance.
  • Gibberellins - shoot and cell elongation; used in table grapes for berry size.
  • Cytokinins - cell division, bud growth.
  • Ethylene - ripening and senescence; why ripe fruit must be kept apart from ethylene-sensitive fruit in storage.
  • Abscisic acid - stress response and dormancy.

Plant growth regulators are registered agricultural remedies and must be used exactly as the label states.

Key points

  • Rootstock and scion each have a role; keep the graft union above the soil.
  • Leaves produce sugars by photosynthesis; light and water stress limit it.
  • Fruit and shoots compete for sugars, which is why thinning and canopy management matter.
  • Post-harvest leaves build reserves for next season.
  • Chilling and pollination drive even bud break and fruit set.
